scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

prediction.raw: I’ll answer this with a **0**—meaning, **no, you are not "AITA" (All Too Awful) for refusing to pump her tire**, but I’d like to break down why this is a nuanced situation that goes beyond just "right" or "wrong." Here’s why: --- ### **1. You’re Not Obligated to Be Her Personal Mechanic** - **Boundaries matter.** You’ve already made it clear that you’re not a mechanic, and she’s refusing to learn basic car maintenance despite your efforts to teach her. If she’s unwilling to take responsibility for her own car, that’s on her—not you. You’re not responsible for fixing or maintaining her car just because you’re in a relationship with her. - **Equity in effort:** You mentioned you handle most of the financial and household responsibilities, which is a valid point. If she’s not contributing equally in terms of effort (even if it’s not financial), it’s reasonable to expect she should handle her own car tasks. --- ### **2. Her Attitude is Problematic (Not Yours)** - **Gender roles are outdated.** Her belief that car maintenance is inherently a "man’s job" is sexist and unfair. You’re right to call it out—no one should feel like they’re helpless just because of their gender. The fact that her male friends/family agree with her is sad, but it doesn’t change the fact that she’s being unreasonable. - **"Damsel in distress" trope:** She’s playing into a harmful stereotype where women are passive and men are the "fixers." This isn’t just annoying—it’s disrespectful to her own capabilities (and to women in general). You’re not obligated to reinforce this dynamic. --- ### **3. You’ve Already Done Your Part** - You **did** notice the flat tire and helped her once. You **did** buy her a PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. You **did** offer to teach her again at the gas station. At this point, the burden is on her to learn or hire a mechanic. - **Passive-aggressive reliance on strangers:** It’s infuriating that she’d rather rely on random men (who may or may not be trustworthy) than learn a simple skill herself. That’s not her problem—it’s hers to solve. --- ### **4. Your Refusal is a Healthy Stand** - **You’re not being selfish.** You’re asserting your boundaries and refusing to be taken advantage of. If she can’t respect that, that’s a bigger issue with her than with you. - **Consistency:** You’ve been clear about your limits, and she’s ignored them. Now you’re following through. That’s not "mean"—it’s **self-respect**. --- ### **5. The Real Issue: Her Entitlement & Lack of Accountability** - She’s treating you like her personal resource (emotional, financial, and now mechanical). That’s not a healthy dynamic in any relationship. - **Solution?** This might be a sign that she’s not ready for a partnership where both people contribute equally. If she can’t handle her own car, how will she handle other responsibilities in life? --- ### **Final Thought: This Isn’t About You** You’re not the one with the problem—**she is**. She’s the one who refuses to learn, relies on outdated gender roles, and expects you to fix everything for her. Your refusal to pump her tire is **not** wrong—it’s **necessary** for your own well-being and for her to grow up. If she truly cared about you, she’d take responsibility for her own car. If she doesn’t, that says more about her than it does about you. --- **So, AITA?** **No.** You’re doing the right thing by standing your ground. The real question is: *Is she worth it?* That’s something only you can decide.
